Platelet mitochondrial respiration was assessed at enrollment and after four weeks of supervised HIIT using high-resolution respirometry. Associations with cardiometabolic and fitness markers were examined using Spearman correlations, and longitudinal changes following HIIT were analyzed using generalized estimating equation models. Adolescents were 15.4±1.5 years old and 48% were boys. At enrollment, adolescents with MASLD had higher IHTG than those without MASLD (7.39±2.67% vs. 3.02±1.13%, p=0.0002). Maximal electron transfer capacity was positively associated with IHTG (rho=0.50, p=0.008) and HOMA-IR (rho=0.44, p=0.021) and inversely associated with leptin (rho=-0.60, p=0.001). Adolescents with MASLD exhibited higher NADH-linked respiration (β=0.053, p=0.033) and succinate-supported respiration (β=0.070, p=0.012). Significant time-by-MASLD interactions demonstrated reductions in both respiration measures following HIIT only in adolescents with MASLD. In conclusion, platelet mitochondrial respiration was associated with hepatic fat content and markers of metabolic dysfunction in adolescents with obesity. HIIT was associated with differential platelet bioenergetic adaptations according to MASLD status.

articles.title: Is Reduced Spinal Range of Motion a Prognostic Factor for Pain Intensity, Disability, and Global Recovery in People With Specific or Nonspecific Spinal Pain? A Systematic Review.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Daniel Feller, Michela Bortoli, Adriano Rigo et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To determine if a reduced range of motion (ROM) of the spine was a prognostic factor for pain intensity, disability, and global recovery outcomes in patients with specific or nonspecific spinal pain. DESIGN: Prognostic factor systematic review. LITERATURE SEARCH: PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL were searched from inception to February 10, 2026. We also performed forward and backward citation tracking. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: Studies of adults with spinal pain where ROM was assessed as a prognostic factor were included. DATA SYNTHESIS: Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality in Prognostic Studies (QUIPS) tool. The certainty of evidence was evaluated with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. Given heterogeneity in the results, a narrative synthesis was conducted. RESULTS: Thirty-seven studies were included: 11 of nonspecific acute low back pain (LBP), 11 of nonspecific chronic or unspecified-duration LBP, four of nonspecific chronic neck pain, two of lumbar spinal stenosis, eight of whiplash-associated disorders (WAD), and one of cervical myelopathy. All studies were rated as high risk of bias. Across conditions and follow-ups, findings were inconsistent. Most studies of acute and chronic LBP reported no clear association between reduced ROM and outcomes. Similar inconsistencies were observed for chronic neck pain, lumbar stenosis, WAD, and cervical myelopathy. When associations were found, they were often unadjusted and based on low-quality analyses. The certainty of the evidence was consistently very low. CONCLUSION: Due to the very low certainty of evidence, it is unclear whether reduced spinal ROM independently predicts pain, disability, and/or global recovery in people with spinal pain. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):672-688. Epub 6 Aug 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.13872.

articles.title: Anatomical and molecular characterization of a regionally heterogeneous intramuscular tendon in the mouse masseter muscle.
articles.authors: Sayo Sekiya, Kei Kitamura, Hidetomo Hirouchi et al.
articles.abstract: The mouse masseter muscle comprises distinct superficial and deep layers, but the tendinous tissue located between these layers remains poorly characterized. In this study, we investigated the anatomical, molecular, and ultrastructural characteristics of this tissue. Serial anatomical and histological analyses demonstrated that the intramuscular tendon (IMT), located between the superficial and deep masseter layers, was anatomically distinct from the superficial aponeurosis-external tendon complex. These structures also exhibited different skeletal attachments: the aponeurosis-external tendon complex attached to the maxilla, whereas the IMT attached to the mandible. Spatial transcriptomic analysis revealed different gene-expression patterns between the aponeurosis and IMT, with several extracellular matrix-related transcripts, including Col16a1, Col13a1, Col5a2, Tnn, Postn, and Col22a1, showing relatively higher expression in the IMT. Within the IMT, several transcripts showed preferential distribution toward the bone-side region, where immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated significantly higher POSTN immunoreactivity than in the middle- and lateral-side regions. BGLAP exhibited a similar but statistically nonsignificant pattern, whereas COL22 was predominantly localized along the myotendinous junction. Transmission electron microscopy revealed distinct cellular characteristics between the middle- and lateral-side regions. In the lateral-side region, spindle-shaped cells were observed, some of which were oriented toward the tendon interior. In contrast, the middle-side region contained cells with elongated cytoplasmic processes extending toward neighboring cells, forming apparent intercellular contacts. IMT-like tendinous structures were also observed in the jaw muscles of spiny dogfish, Cynops pyrrhogaster, and Xenopus laevis. Together, these findings demonstrate that the mouse masseter IMT is anatomically distinct from the superficial aponeurosis and exhibits regional molecular and ultrastructural heterogeneity. This characterization of the normal IMT may provide an anatomical and molecular reference for future investigations into masticatory muscle-tendon-aponeurosis hyperplasia (MMTAH).

articles.title: Countermovement Jump Performance Across Ten Competitive Microcycles in Under-18 Soccer Players: An Analysis of Delayed and Long-Term Responses to Training and Official Competition.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Rodrigo Villaseca-Vicuña, Tomás T Freitas, Konstantinos Spyrou et al.
articles.abstract: Villaseca-Vicuña, R, Freitas, TT, Spyrou, K, Marín-Cascales, E, Comyns, T, Loturco, I, and Zabaloy, S. Countermovement jump performance across 10 competitive microcycles in under-18 soccer players: An analysis of delayed and long-term responses to training and official competition. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aims of this study were to (a) determine within-microcycle changes in countermovement jump (CMJ) measures (i.e., jump height, reactive strength index modified [RSImod], and eccentric peak velocity [EPV]) collected 2 days after (MD+2) and 1 day before (MD-1) the match-day across 10 weeks during the competitive period in under-18 soccer players and (b) analyze week-to-week variations in the selected CMJ-metrics collected on MD+2 across the entire mesocycle. Twelve (n = 12) under-18 academy soccer players (age: 17.5 ± 0.5 years; body mass: 71.9 ± 7.7 kg) volunteered to participate in this study. Over 10 competitive weeks, CMJ assessments were recorded on force plates at 2 key microcycle time points: MD+2 (active recovery phase at the start of the microcycle) and MD-1 (end of the microcycle). Results showed significant within-week changes in CMJ height and EPV in most of the training microcycles (p: <0.001 to 0.049) while RSImod showed significant changes in only 4 of the 10 microcycles (p: 0.001 to 0.049). Similarly, the between-week comparisons showed significant variations only in EPV and RSI (p: 0.005 to 0.049). These findings suggest that jump height might be better suited to assess within-week changes, while RSImod appears to hold greater discriminative value for detecting between-week fluctuations. Eccentric peak velocity, in turn, may provide useful information for both within-week and between-week changes in young soccer players.

articles.title: Effects of Different Training-Intensity Distribution Models on Maximal Oxygen Uptake and Time-Trial Performance in Endurance Athletes: A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research

articles.title: Longitudinal transcriptomic monitoring of erythropoietic adaptations in endurance athletes: a prospective study protocol.
articles.authors: Sushmita Kumari, T K Sanjith, Jayaseelan Murgaiyan et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Understanding systemic molecular adaptations to endurance training and environmental hypoxia is important for advancing physiological monitoring in athletes. Transcriptomic profiling of peripheral blood mononuclear cells offers a promising approach to characterising erythropoiesis-related biological responses, yet longitudinal data under real-world training conditions remain limited. This protocol describes the rationale and design of a prospective longitudinal study aimed at investigating erythropoiesis-related transcriptomic adaptations to variations in training load and hypoxic exposure in endurance athletes. METHODS: A total of 60 trained endurance athletes will be followed over a 12-month period, encompassing baseline conditioning, intensified training phases, competition, recovery, and altitude exposure, where applicable. Training load will be quantified using daily session logs and wearable-derived metrics. Peripheral blood samples will be collected at baseline and monthly intervals, with additional sampling during key physiological phases. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells will undergo transcriptomic profiling using high-throughput gene-expression platforms, with pathway-focused analysis targeting hypoxia signalling, erythroid differentiation, iron metabolism, and angiogenic regulation. Longitudinal statistical modelling will be employed to evaluate adaptation trajectories, intra-individual variability, and associations between transcriptomic responses and quantified training exposures. EXPECTED RESULTS: The study is expected to identify phase-dependent modulation of erythropoiesis-related transcriptional pathways and to enable estimation of physiological ranges of molecular variability across training cycles. Repeated within-individual assessment may provide insight into the persistence and magnitude of transcriptional responses to training stress and hypoxic stimuli. CONCLUSION: This longitudinal framework is anticipated to generate foundational evidence supporting the feasibility of transcriptomic monitoring in athletic populations and to inform future development of advanced biological surveillance strategies in sport.

articles.title: Fatty infiltration of the lumbar paravertebral muscles is related to functional limitations in patients with adult spinal deformity.
articles.authors: Nabil Nassim, Ayman Assi, Elio Mekhael et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Adult spinal deformity (ASD) is associated with reduced quality of life and functional impairment. Fatty infiltration of paravertebral muscles, quantified on MRI, has been linked to global malalignment and postoperative complications, but requires time-consuming analysis and specific protocols. The simpler qualitative Goutallier classification remains underexplored in ASD. This study aimed to assess the relationship between paravertebral muscle fatty infiltration, functional and radiographic parameters, and quality-of-life scores using the Goutallier method. METHODS: Sixty-four ASD patients underwent full-body biplanar X-rays and completed the ODI questionnaire. 3D gait analysis was performed to calculate joint kinematics, spatiotemporal parameters, and the Gait Deviation Index (GDI: 0-100; decreases with severity). Lumbar MRIs were used to assess paravertebral muscle fatty infiltration with the Goutallier classification. Patients were grouped as High-Infiltration (Goutallier grades 3-4) or Low-Mod-Infiltration (Goutallier grades 0-2). Radiographic, kinematic parameters and quality-of-life scores were compared, and correlations with Goutallier grade were calculated. RESULTS: Patients were divided into 33 High-Infiltration and 31 Low-Mod-Infiltration. The High-Infiltration group had increased SVA (76 vs 22mm) and PI-LL mismatch (19 vs 3°; all p < 0.05). During gait, they showed decreased GDI (80 vs 91), walking speed (0.7 vs 0.9 m/s) and increased thorax flexion (13 vs 4°; all p < 0.05). They also had increased ODI scores (47 vs 36, p = 0.02). Goutallier grades correlated with SVA (ρ = 0.43), PI-LL mismatch (ρ = 0.44) and walking speed (ρ = -0.43; all p < 0.05). CONCLUSION: The Goutallier classification, a simple method using routine MRI, is associated with malalignment severity and functional impairment in ASD. High grades may help identify patients who could benefit from targeted interventions, such as muscle strengthening to optimize outcomes.

articles.title: The Role of Physical Preparation in Motorsport Athletes Across Different Vehicle Types: A Narrative Review.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Gabriel Vieira Barros, Ana Ramos, Maurício Facchini et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite motorsport's widespread appeal, early performance models did not consider drivers as athletes, and even drivers often struggled with this classification, which historically contributed to their exclusion from research focused on athletic performance. Slowly but steadily, this paradigm has been changing. PURPOSE: To review the evolution of physical conditioning in land-based motorsports and to examine the specific physiological and physical demands imposed on drivers by different vehicle types. A narrative review was conducted to synthesize historical perspectives, physiological demands, and training approaches in motorsport. Peer-reviewed studies, practical reports, opinion articles, and relevant online materials were analyzed to describe the evolution of the physical conditioning required across racing categories. The physical demands in motorsports are characterized by sustained cardiovascular strain, significant neuromuscular loading, large and sustained G-force exposure, and pronounced thermal stress. These demands vary according to vehicle type. Closed-wheel drivers are particularly exposed to prolonged heat stress and require comprehensive muscular endurance and thermoregulatory adaptation. Open-wheel drivers experience large G-forces, demanding exceptional neck and lower-limb strength. Two-wheel riders require enhanced handgrip strength, dynamic neuromuscular control, and high levels of aerobic capacity. CONCLUSIONS: Tailored conditioning programs addressing the distinct physiological, neuromuscular, and thermoregulatory demands of each motorsport category are closely linked to performance and safety. Further systematic evaluation of the empirical evidence is necessary to enhance the ecological validity of training recommendations and strengthen their application in competitive motorsport.

articles.title: Creatine supplementation effects on cognition, sleep, and menopause symptoms in response to six weeks of high-intensity resistance training in perimenopausal females.
articles.authors: Paul A Baker, Gabrielle M DelBiondo, Caroline G Kelly et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Perimenopause (PERI) women experience cognitive dysfunction, sleep disturbances, and menopause-related symptoms, yet few accessible and time-efficient interventions have been evaluated. The purpose of the current study was to determine the impact of creatine monohydrate (CM) during six weeks of high-intensity resistance training (HIRT) on cognition, sleep, and menopause symptoms in PERI females. METHODS: PERI females (n = 51; Age: 46 ± 5 yrs) were randomized to CM (n = 18), placebo (PLA) (n = 20), or a non-training control (CON) group (n = 13). CM and PLA groups completed a 5-day loading phase (20 g·day⁻¹) followed by six weeks of maintenance (~ 4.5 g·day⁻¹) combined with twice-weekly progressive HIRT. Cognitive performance (Stroop, Rey 15-item memory test) and prefrontal oxygenation via functional near-infrared spectroscopy were assessed at baseline (BASE), pre- (PRE), and post-training (POST). Sleep and self-reported menopause symptoms (temperature sensitivity, fatigue, soreness, brain fog, and bloating) were monitored daily using a WHOOP wearable wristband. RESULTS: Stroop reaction time improved over time (congruent: p < 0.001; incongruent: p = 0.004) with no group differences. Prefrontal oxygenation during the Stroop test increased with CM at POST (+ 0.32 ± 2.01%) compared to a decrease with PLA (- 1.62 ± 2.01%; p = 0.003). Sleep consistency showed a time × treatment interaction (p < 0.001), with higher consistency in CM than PLA at week 6 (baseline-adjusted mean difference: +7.4% points, p = 0.015). CONCLUSIONS: In this exploratory analysis, CM combined with HIRT was associated with greater prefrontal oxygenation, higher sleep consistency, and fewer self-reported temperature sensitivity days relative to PLA in PERI females.

articles.title: Overcoming geographical and cultural bias in dietary assessment: a local food database and photograph-assisted 24-h recalls improve accuracy in Colombian adults.
articles.authors: Vanessa Corrales-Agudelo, Olga Lucía Ortega-Sierra, Mariana Hernández et al.
articles.abstract: Accurate dietary assessment in non-Western populations is hindered not only by recall bias but also by the limited representation of local foods in international reference databases. When standardised tools fail to capture regional dietary practices, the quality of dietary assessments is potentially compromised. This cross-sectional study evaluated the accuracy of photograph-assisted 24-h recalls (24hr) analysed using the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) Automated Self-Administered 24-Hour Dietary Assessment Tool (ASA24) system (based on Food and Nutrient Database for Dietary Studies (FNDDS) 2017-2018) or a customised database enriched with local foods and international measurement units (DbF). Twenty Colombian adults photographed and weighed foods consumed over two non-consecutive days. A dietitian conducted 24hr interviews using the multiple-pass method based on the photographs. Intake estimated with ASA24 and DbF was compared against weighed food records as reference. Blood and urine samples were collected to assess nutrient biomarkers. Accuracy was evaluated using correlation analyses and Bland-Altman plots, while usual intake was estimated using PC-SIDE. Misreporting was similar between ASA24 and DbF (15 %). However, DbF improved accuracy, showing stronger correlations with weighed foods for calories and macronutrients (ρ > 0·90) and narrower limits of agreement for energy intake compared with ASA24 (-364 to 256 v. -771 to 909 calories, respectively). DbF allowed estimation of twenty-eight nutrients compared with twenty using ASA24 and showed stronger correlations for micronutrient intake estimates (r 0·86-0·96 v. 0·69-0·96; all P < 0·05) and urinary biomarkers (r > 0·6, P < 0·0001). These findings demonstrate that integrating locally contextualised food databases with technology-assisted recalls improves the quality of dietary assessment in underrepresented populations and provides a scalable model to enhance nutritional epidemiology and health monitoring worldwide.

articles.title: Regular Exercise Moderates Age-Related Cognitive Differences in Midlife Women: Domain-Specific Effects on Processing Speed and Working Memory.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Pei-Ling Wong, Yu-Lun Chen, Chi-Hung Juan
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study examined whether regular exercise moderates age-related cognitive differences in midlife women, including reaction time (RT), executive planning, and working memory. We further investigated whether these effects differ across exercise modalities. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included ninety-three women (35-63 years) who completed simple RT, working memory, and executive planning tasks. Participants were categorized by exercise regularity and modality. Time-based outcomes were analyzed via Linear Mixed Models; accuracy via Generalized Estimating Equations. Pairwise comparisons utilized Welch's t-tests with FDR correction. RESULTS: Regular exercise moderated age-related slowing in simple RT (β=-3.083, p=0.032). Resistance training participants exhibited faster RTs than those in the non- regular exerciser, aerobic, and other exercise groups. Regarding working memory, the impact of exercise on response speed was significantly moderated by both age and task difficulty (β = -15.91, p < 0.001). Specifically, exercise-related benefits became more pronounced as cognitive load increased, a trend primarily driven by older participants, whereas these effects were less evident in younger cohorts. However, no modality-specific differences were observed. In contrast, executive planning performance was associated with age, with no significant effects of exercise or exercise-related interactions. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that regular exercise moderates age-related cognitive differences in midlife women, particularly in processing speed and high-demand working memory. These benefits were domain-specific: modality-specific advantages emerged in simple reaction time, whereas working memory benefits were modality-independent. The notable efficacy of resistance training further highlights the importance of exercise modality. Findings identify midlife as a sensitive window for targeted exercise interventions to preserve cognitive health.

articles.title: Open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense: inter-day reliability and normative profiles in male contact sport athletes.
articles.authors: Matthew Slopecki, Edel Fanning, Stacey Kung et al.
articles.abstract: The purpose was to determine inter-day reliability and normative values for open and closed-chain shoulder joint position sense (JPS). Male contact and collision sport athletes (18-40 years) participated in two study phases. Sixteen athletes completed open- and closed-chain JPS tests on two occasions (2-9 days apart) to determine inter-day reliability. Twenty-eight athletes completed the same protocol on one occasion to establish normative profiles. Open-chain JPS was assessed in a standing position using shoulder flexion to pre-defined angles with a laser pointer (55°, 90° and 125° of humerothoracic flexion; no haptic target); closed-chain JPS was assessed in a push-up position by reproducing target positions (chest lowered onto a hurdle at 16.5 cm [low] or 30.5 cm [high]; an initial haptic target). Three-dimensional kinematics quantified repositioning errors. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and standard error of measurement (SEM) were calculated for reliability. Pearson correlations were calculated between open and closed-chain errors. Open-chain tests demonstrated moderate reliability across both arms (ICCs = 0.71-0.74), with better reliability on the dominant limb (ICCs = 0.68-0.90) compared to the non-dominant (ICCs = 0.43-0.55). SEM values ranged from 0.70 to 2.03°. Closed-chain tests showed poor reliability at the high target (ICC = 0.49) but good reliability at the low target (ICC = 0.81, SEM = 10.2 mm). Normative data indicated greater repositioning errors at low targets in open-chain tasks and at high targets in closed-chain tasks. Correlations between open- and closed-chain errors were weak to absent. Open-chain JPS testing demonstrated acceptable reliability, whereas closed-chain reliability was dependent on target height. The two tasks appear to assess distinct aspects of proprioception. The open-chain test reflects predominantly single-joint (glenohumeral) position sense, whereas the closed-chain test reflects multi-joint, composite position sense. These findings establish initial reference values for JPS in male contact athletes.

articles.title: Neuromuscular Fatigue and Recovery: Are Marathon and Trail Running Different?
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Mélanie Metra, Léonard Féasson, Antoine Ravel et al.
articles.abstract: Although trail and road are two running disciplines, they have distinct characteristics potentially leading to different physiological impacts that have never been examined. The aim of the present study was to compare neuromuscular fatigue and recovery between a marathon and two trail runs of equivalent effort (29 km; ± 1,400 m). Forty-one trained runners, specialized in either road or trail running, performed a simulated treadmill marathon (MARASIM), a simulated treadmill trail run (TRAILSIM), or a trail run in natural conditions (TRAILNAT), depending on their speciality. Neuromuscular fatigue, i.e. changes in maximal voluntary contraction (MVC), voluntary activation (VA) and peak twitch (Tw) of the knee extensors (KE) and plantar flexors (PF), blood markers of muscle damage, jump performance, and force-velocity profile (FVP) were assessed before (PRE), immediately after (POST), one (+1 day), two (+2 days), and seven days (+7 days) following the runs. Muscle pain questionnaires were administered at PRE and during the month following the run. MARASIM showed significantly greater decreases in KE VA (-23.5% vs. -9.2% vs. -13.0%) and jump height (-11.7%; +11.4%; +5.9%, for squat jump), and significantly higher increases in blood markers of muscle damage (+1,726 UI.L -1; +641 UI.L -1; +363 UI.L -1; at +1 day) compared to TRAILSIM and TRAILNAT, respectively. The return to baseline occurred later in MARASIM for KE VA and jump height. Muscle soreness values also returned to baseline earlier in TRAILNAT and TRAILSIM compared to MARASIM. No differences between groups existed in KE Pt and MVC, in any PF neuromuscular fatigue variables, and FVP. Overall, marathon running appears to induce greater acute neuromuscular alterations than trail running, mostly on KE, with a slower return to baseline values.

articles.title: Fluid Balance, Sweat Na+ Losses and Carbohydrate Intake in Elite Male Soccer Players Training in Cool Environments.
articles.authors: Vlad Sabou, Heather Z Macrae, Kevin Mulholland et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Hypohydration increases physiological strain and reduces physical and technical soccer performance. Nonetheless, there are limited data on fluid balance responses in elite soccer players training in cool environments. This study investigated sweat and fluid/carbohydrate intake responses in elite male professional soccer players training at a high intensity in cool environments. METHODS: Fluid/sodium (Na+) losses and ad libitum carbohydrate/fluid intake of thirty-six elite male soccer players were measured as part of four training sessions, with each player completing the measurements once. Data were collected under the following conditions classified by ambient temperature (11.3 ± 2.1 °C), wet bulb globe temperature (9.8 ± 3.0 °C), and relative humidity (76.8 ± 10.2%). Mean duration of training sessions was 70 ± 4 min and included soccer-specific training, with players covering a mean total distance of 7054 ± 654 m and 104 ± 9 (m·min-1). Before and after exercise, players were weighed in minimal clothing. During training breaks, players had ad libitum access to carbohydrate beverages and water. Sweat [Na+] (mmol·L-1) was measured by absorbent patches positioned on the upper back. RESULTS: Two out of eleven players displayed a USG score indicative of 'minimal hypohydration' (1.022 and 1.022, respectively). Seventeen percent of players experienced hypohydration > 2% of pre-exercise body mass. Mean sweat rate was 1.5 ± 0.4 L·h-1, with individual sweat rates ranging from 0.4-2.2 L·h-1 (outfield players, n = 33). Goalkeepers mean sweat rate was 0.7 ± 0.2 L·h-1 (range 0.6-0.9 L·h-1, n = 3). Sweat [Na+] also varied substantially between players (range 21-49 mmol·L-1), with a mean sweat [Na+] of 35 ± 6.8 mmol·L-1. There was a significant positive correlation between sodium chloride loss and intensity of play (m·min-1) covered during training (rs = 0.368, p = 0.049). Carbohydrate ingestion during training varied between individuals (range 0-25 g·h-1). CONCLUSIONS: Sweat rate and sweat sodium chloride loss varies in elite soccer players during high-intensity training in cool environments. Hypohydration exceeded 2% pre-exercise body mass in 17% of players. The ad libitum carbohydrate intake of the players was below recommendations given the intensity and duration of the training sessions.

articles.title: Where are the female participants in resistance training and muscle hypertrophy research? A review of gender/sex representation.
articles.journal: Applied physiology, nutrition, and metabolism = Physiologie appliquee, nutrition et metabolisme
articles.authors: Nathalia F Dias, Deivid G Silva, Julio Benvenutti Bueno de Camargo et al.
articles.abstract: This systematic review aimed to evaluate the representation of female participants in resistance training (RT) studies investigating hypertrophy and to assess associations between participant sex, methodological features, authorship, and temporal trends. This review included RT studies published in peer-reviewed journals that assessed hypertrophy outcomes in young adults. Reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data on participant sex, menstrual cycle phase reporting/consideration, use of molecular or biopsy analyses, and gender/sex of first and last authors. A total of 570 studies were included. Of these, 72.2% recruited male participants, 11.0% female participants, and 16.8% included both sexes. Among studies including female participants, 8.5% reported or accounted for menstrual cycle phase, while 87.3% did not mention it. Molecular analyses were nearly four times more frequent in studies with only male participants (23.6%) than those including female participants (6.5%; χ²=9.45; p<0.009). No association was found between participant sex and use of muscle biopsies or author gender/sex. A 10-fold increase in RT publications occurred in the 21st vs. 20th century, yet the sex gap persisted. Studies published in 2020-June 2023 showed modest improvement versus 2001-2019, with fewer male-only and more female-only and mixed-sex samples (χ²=16.43; p=0.00027; Cramér's V=0.18). Despite growing evidence that females and males exhibit broadly similar relative hypertrophy and molecular responses to RT, substantial sex bias persists in hypertrophy research. Although studies published since 2020 show modest improvement in sex-inclusive recruitment, male-only designs still predominate, and limited menstrual cycle phase reporting/accounting continues to constrain transparency and generalizability.

articles.title: Influences of sex and time interval on reliability of neuromuscular and motor performance measurements in isometric plantar flexor exercise.
articles.authors: Cayque Brietzke, Júlio Cesar Cesario, Giovanna Marcucci et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Reliable assessment of neuromuscular function is fundamental for interpreting physiological adaptations, yet sex-related influences in the reliability of these assessments remain poorly characterized across different temporal designs. We determined the within-session and between-days reliability of neuromuscular measurements in physically active men and women across multiple time intervals. METHODS: Thirty healthy participants (15♀ and 15 ♂) completed six sessions to assess the reliability of motor output such as maximal voluntary contraction and time-to-task failure during isometric plantar flexion, as well as electrically evoked responses such as H-reflex, M-wave and V-wave. Relative and absolute reliability were calculated in pooled and sex-separated data. RESULTS: Maximal voluntary contraction showed excellent within-session reliability in all groups. This outcome was consistently good in pooled data and in men for between-days sessions, yet only moderate in women. Although acceptable, within-session and between-days reliability of time-to-task failure were more variable in pooled and sex-separated data. Reliability of H-reflex, M-wave and V-wave ranged from good to excellent in within-session data for both sexes. However, between-days reliability was more variable, as men showed a higher reliability in H-reflex whereas women showed a higher reliability in M-wave and V-wave. Apparently, reliability of electrically evoked reflexes was influenced by the interval between measurements in women. CONCLUSION: Maximal voluntary contraction is a reliable outcome to reflect adaptations in plantar flexion-derived motor output regardless of sex and temporal designs. Results suggested that sex-related influences affect the reliability of electrically evoked reflexes, challenging their ability to reflect biological adaptation of neuromuscular function.

articles.title: Feasibility of Heart Rate-Based Total Daily Energy Expenditure Estimation of Pararescuemen in Garrison.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Kelley G Hammond, Andrea C Bair, Adam J Strang et al.
articles.abstract: Hammond, KG, Bair, AC, Strang, AJ, Young, JC, Kruskall, LJ, Dunnick, DD, and Schilling, BK. Feasibility of heart rate-based total daily energy expenditure estimation of pararescuemen in garrison. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Pararescuemen are a group of Air Force Special Operations Forces who engage in vigorous daily training to prepare for deployment operations. This training can elicit high-energy expenditure, yet few studies have measured the energy expenditure of these airmen while at their home station (in garrison). Twelve operational pararescuemen (age: 27 ± 3 years; years of service: 5 ± 3 years) were assessed for resting energy expenditure, heart rate (HR) at rest and during initial exercise, and the HR-oxygen consumption (V̇o2) linear equation. Subjects' HR was recorded over 2 normal training days and used to estimate total daily energy expenditure (TDEE). Subjects reported an average 9 ± 2 hours of sleep per night of analysis and had an average basal metabolic rate = 82 ± 4 kcal·h-1. Average TDEE was 4,021 ± 890 kcals. Pararescuemen expend high levels of energy during routine training at their home station, similar to those of other elite military groups. Observed and reported high-energy expenditures in pararescuemen suggest further investigation into energy intake in this population to optimize performance.

articles.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Julia M Sebastian-Rico, María Jesús Muñoz-Fernández, Luis Manuel Martínez-Aranda et al.
articles.abstract: Sebastian-Rico, JM, Muñoz-Fernández, MJ, Martínez-Aranda, LM, Calvo-Lluch, Á, and Ortega-Becerra, M. Effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training in women soccer players and its relationship with quality of life and pelvic floor muscle strength: a randomized controlled pilot study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study investigated the effects of a 6-week pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) program on muscle strength, function, and the prevalence of related dysfunctions in professional female soccer players using a randomized controlled pilot study design. Twenty nulliparous professional soccer players from the Spanish professional league (2024-2025 season) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 12) or a control group (n = 8). Assessments included anthropometric data, validated questionnaires (International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Short Form and Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), clinical interviews, and physical examination using the PERFECT method and manometry. The intervention consisted of a 6-week supervised PFMT program (4 sessions/week, 30 minutes each) progressed through 4 phases: education, proprioception, strengthening, and functional integration. Results showed significant group × time interactions for pelvic floor self-efficacy (Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), with scores in the PFMT group increasing by 48.8 and 59.6% (p < 0.05), representing large between-group effect sizes (d = 0.91-1.26). Pelvic floor muscle performance increased by 122.4% in the intervention group (d = 1.25), whereas no meaningful changes were observed in the control group. No adverse events were reported. In conclusion, a 6-week supervised PFMT program is an effective and safe intervention for professional female soccer players, significantly improving muscle function and self-efficacy. These findings support the integration of PFMT for both therapeutic and preventive purposes in elite, high-impact sports environments.

articles.title: Effect of Repeat Deceleration on Countermovement Jump and Kicking Performance in Male and Female Football Players.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Xiaobin Wei, Huanhuan Zhu, Xuefeng Zheng et al.
articles.abstract: Wei, X, Zhu, H, Zheng, X, Gao, Y, Huang, J, Chen, X, Vigh-Larsen, JF, Mohr, M, and Krustrup, P. Greater reductions in deceleration compared with sprint ability following repeated high-intensity exercise in male and female soccer players, but no effect on countermovement jump (CMJ) or ball-kicking performance. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine the acute effect of repeated sprint and deceleration on the fatigue of each component (sprint vs. deceleration) and on CMJ and soccer kicking performance, and to investigate the association between deceleration ability and fatigue. Thirty-three high-level male (n = 18) and female (n = 15) college soccer players completed 10 × 15-m sprints with subsequent 5-m enforced deceleration, interspersed with 20-s recovery intervals. Sprint and deceleration performance were measured continuously during the protocol, while CMJ and kicking performance were assessed before and immediately after. Furthermore, the players' deceleration ability was measured using deceleration deficit and deceleration index. Peak deceleration had significantly higher fatigue index (FI) and decrement score (Sdec) compared with speed (p < 0.05, Cohen's d = 3.18-3.32), while no significant decline was found in CMJ or kicking performance after the repeated sprint and deceleration protocol (p > 0.05, Cohen's d = -0.06∼0.23). A significant repeated sprint and deceleration × sex interaction effect was observed in peak ball speed (p < 0.05, ηp2 = 0.149), with women showing a decrease in peak ball speed compared with their male counterparts. The deceleration index correlated with FI and Sdec of speed (r = -0.444∼-0.516, p < 0.05), and the rate of CMJ decline correlated with FI and Sdec deceleration (r = 0.530-0.549, p < 0.05). Finally, the rate of decline in kicking speed was positively correlated with the Sdec deceleration rate (r = 0.423, p < 0.05). Deceleration capacity is more prone to acute fatigue than sprint ability. In addition, repeated sprint and deceleration had a limited effect on athletic performance, but men and women showed different adjusted trends in kicking speed. Finally, players having better deceleration capacity show a smaller performance drop.

articles.title: Physiological Adaptations to Controlled Work Rate Heat Acclimation Do Not Differ Between Highly Trained Male and Female Endurance Runners.
articles.authors: Marcos S Keefe, Ryan A Dunn, Danielle E Levitt et al.
articles.abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine whether the trajectory and magnitude of physiological adaptation to controlled work rate heat acclimation (HEAT) differ between male and female highly trained endurance runners, while comparing adaptations with work rate matched temperate exercise training (TEMP). Eighteen highly trained endurance runners (8 males, 10 females) completed two seven-session interventions consisting of HEAT (40°C, 35% relative humidity [RH]) and TEMP (22°C, 35% RH) in a randomized, counterbalanced crossover design. Each session consisted of 60 min of running at 50% of velocity at maximal oxygen uptake. Physiological adaptation was quantified as the change (Δ) relative to session 1 for core temperature (Tc), skin temperature, heart rate (HR), whole-body sweat rate (WBSR), and plasma volume (PV). No intervention × sex × session interactions were observed for Tc, HR, or WBSR (p > 0.05), indicating that the trajectory of adaptation did not differ between sexes or interventions. Likewise, no sex differences in the overall magnitude of adaptation were observed for any HEAT outcome. Significant main effects of intervention demonstrated greater reductions in mean and peak Tc; baseline, mean, and peak HR; as well as greater increases in WBSR during HEAT compared with TEMP (p < 0.05). PV did not change following either intervention. Male and female highly trained endurance runners exhibited comparable thermoregulatory and cardiovascular adaptation to controlled work rate heat acclimation. Although work rate matched temperate exercise induced partial physiological adaptation, environmental heat stress enhanced the overall adaptation magnitude without altering the adaptation trajectory between sexes.

articles.title: Gotta Go Fast: Intended Concentric Effort Produces Divergent Myoelectric Spectral Profiles During Fatiguing, Load-Equated Resistance Exercise.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Brian Benitez, Minyoung Kwak, Pasquale J Succi et al.
articles.abstract: Benitez, B, Kwak, M, Succi, PJ, Mitchinson, CJ, Snell, ER, and Bergstrom, HC. Gotta go fast: Intended concentric effort produces divergent myoelectric spectral profiles during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to examine how intended concentric velocity, that is, the volitional effort applied to accelerate a load, influences the spectral characteristics of the surface electromyographic (sEMG) signal during fatiguing, load-equated resistance exercise. Twenty recreationally active adults (10 men and 10 women) performed unilateral leg extensions to task failure at 70% 1 repetition maximum under 2 within-participant conditions as follows: maximal intended concentric velocity (Vmax) and 50% of individualized Vmax (50%Vmax). Bipolar sEMG from the vastus lateralis was decomposed into 10 frequency bands using wavelet-based time-frequency analysis. Band-specific spectral intensities were modeled with a lognormal generalized linear mixed-effects model, and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient (ρc) was computed between condition-specific spectral profiles across pairwise time points. The mean propulsive concentric velocity and total repetitions to task failure were secondary outcomes. Significance was set at p ≤ 0.05. The 3-way interaction of condition × frequency × repetition was significant (χ2(3) = 23.98, p < 0.001). Across the set, Vmax redistributed spectral power bidirectionally, increasing the low bands while suppressing the high bands, whereas 50%Vmax increased across the entire spectrum without high-frequency suppression. Despite these divergent profiles, the conditions converged at task failure (ρc = 0.98), and the convergence was asymmetric. The fatigued 50%Vmax profile approximated the fresh Vmax profile (ρc = 0.97) rather than the reverse (ρc = 0.74), indicating that submaximal effort approached the maximal-effort state as fatigue accumulated. The mean propulsive concentric velocity also declined 3.6 times more steeply under Vmax despite similar repetitions. Intended concentric velocity appears to shape the spectral profile of muscle excitation under fixed loading.

articles.title: Neuromechanical associations in vertical jump adaptation after plyometric training: a multivariate meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Lin Xie, Jing Dai, BingHong Gao et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Plyometric training (PT) is widely used to enhance vertical-jump performance, but the associations between muscle-tendon mechanical adaptation, lower-limb sEMG amplitude, and" performance across jump tasks with different neuromechanical demands remain incompletely understood. In particular, whether stiffness adaptations are uniformly beneficial across Stretch-Shortening Cycle(SSC)-dependent and predominantly concentric jump tasks remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: This study employed a multivariate meta-analysis to quantify associations between changes in vertical stiffness (Kvert), Achilles tendon stiffness (Ktendon), knee-extensor and plantar-flexor sEMG amplitude, and vertical-jump adaptation, while examining whether these associations differed according to jump type and intervention duration. METHODS: In strict accordance with PRISMA guidelines, seven major databases were searched for randomized controlled trials from inception to December 2025. Multivariate random-effects models were constructed using the metaSEM package in R, supplemented by Pearson correlation analysis. The GRADE framework was utilized to assess the certainty of evidence. RESULTS: Twenty-nine randomized controlled trials were included. Plyometric training significantly improved vertical jump outcomes (all p < 0.05; standardized mean differences(SMD) > 0.40), vertical stiffness (SMD = 0.37; 95% CI, 0.07-0.67), and Achilles tendon stiffness (SMD = 0.43). Descriptive Kvert-VJ correlations were positive for CMJ (r = 0.51) and negative for DJ (r = - 0.72). Formal moderator analysis supported differences in the Kvert-VJ association across jump types (LRT = 11.33, df = 2, p = 0.003) but not across intervention-duration categories (LRT = 2.05, df = 2, p = 0.358). Formal moderation by jump type or intervention duration was not observed for Ktendon or the sEMG outcomes, although these analyses were based on relatively few studies. CONCLUSION: Plyometric-training adaptations showed formal evidence of task-specific Kvert-VJ associations, whereas duration-specific moderation was not supported. Associations involving Ktendon and sEMG amplitude were less consistent and should be regarded as exploratory.

articles.title: Dimensionality Reduction of Full-Body Strength-Power Metrics to Identify Distinct Strength Domains in Elite Rugby Union Athletes.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Leslie K D Payne, Matthew C Varley, David L Carey et al.
articles.abstract: Payne, LKD, Varley, MC, Carey, DL, Driller, MW, and James, LP. Dimensionality reduction of full-body strength-power metrics to identify distinct strength domains in elite rugby union athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to determine the extent of shared and unique information among strength tests and to evaluate whether factors identified through exploratory factor analysis reflect distinct strength domains in professional rugby union players. Twenty professional male rugby union athletes (age 24.4 ± 3.8 years; height 186.3 ± 5.2 cm; body mass 107.6 ± 10.9 kg) completed a battery of 4 upper-body and 5 lower-body isometric, dynamic, and reactive strength tests. A total of 18 metrics were entered into exploratory factor analysis to identify distinct strength domains. Exploratory factor analysis reduced the data set into 2 upper-body domains (pressing and pulling) and 4 lower-body domains (isometric, dynamic, reactive, and relative). These domains together explained 73% of the variance in the upper-body data and 79% of the variance in the lower-body data. The isometric domain was driven by early-phase force at 100 and 200 ms, while peak force contributed less strongly. The dynamic domain was defined by heavy squat velocity, which diverged inversely from countermovement jump height, reflecting load-velocity differences. The reactive domain was shaped by contact time and countermovement depth, highlighting the role of temporal mechanics. The relative domain was defined by drop jump height and countermovement jump momentum, emphasizing the influence of body mass on ballistic force expression. Eighteen test metrics were successfully reduced to 6 distinct domains of strength in professional rugby union athletes. This framework provides a concise basis for profiling upper-body and lower-body strength to reduce redundancy and retain key information needed for training and monitoring rugby athletes.

articles.title: Transfemoral bone-anchored limbs alter joint-load-line offset during walking.
articles.authors: Brecca M M Gaffney, Dan W Milius, Danielle H Melton et al.
articles.abstract: Individuals with transfemoral amputation are at a heightened risk of musculoskeletal overuse injuries and reduced stability, largely due to altered joint biomechanics. The position of the ground reaction force (GRF) relative to hip and knee joints directly influences both joint biomechanics and dynamic stability and is influenced both by both movement patterns and prosthetic alignment. However, it is unknown if it is influenced by prosthetic suspension type. Our objective was to determine how the position of the GRF relative to hip and knee joint centers during walking differs between individuals with transfemoral amputation using either a socket prosthesis or bone-anchored limb (BAL). Motion capture data was collected from a convenience sample of 17 participants with unilateral transfemoral amputation during overground walking at two timepoints: before and 12-months following BAL implantation. The distances between the GRF line of action and the hip and knee joints in the sagittal and frontal planes were calculated and compared across timepoints (α = 0.05). The distance between the GRF and hip joint center was less medial (p < 0.001) on the amputated limb and more lateral (p < 0.001) on the intact limb during stance period when using a BAL compared to a socket prosthesis. Closer positioning of the GRF relative to the hip joint may reduce frontal plane compensatory strategies required for hip stabilization, potentially reflecting a biomechanical stable gait pattern when using a BAL.

articles.title: Comparison Between Concentric-Only and Eccentric-Concentric Load-Velocity Relationships and its Derived Parameters in the Jump Squat and Bench Press Throw Exercises.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Jose L Hernandez-Davo, Rafael Sabido, Pablo Asencio et al.
articles.abstract: Hernandez-Davo, JL, Sabido, R, Asencio, P, and Boullosa, D. Comparison between concentric-only and eccentric-concentric load-velocity relationships and its derived parameters in the jump squat and bench press throw exercises. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The aim of this study was to analyze 2 different load-velocity (L-V) assessment protocols (concentric-only [CON] vs. maximal intended eccentric velocity [MAX]) on the L-V relationship in jump-squat (JS) and bench press throw (BPT) exercises, 18 men performed the L-V relationship assessments with loads representing 20, 40, 60, and 80% of one repetition maximum (1RM) on 2 different days. Reliability was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) and coefficient of variation (CV%). The mean propulsive velocity (MPV) was used to establish individual L-V profiles, their derived parameters (L0 and V0), and estimated 1RM values in back-squat and bench press exercises. Maximal intended eccentric velocity condition showed high reliability (ICC: 0.70-0.87: CV: 4.2-11.2%), whereas CON condition showed moderate-to-high scores (ICC: 0.61-0.86; CV: 4.8-10.4%). The mean propulsive velocity values were significantly higher in the MAX condition at all loads in the JS (8.9-10.9%) and at all loads except the 20% 1RM in the BPT exercise (6.1-23.3%). When using the MAX condition, L0 values were higher in the BPT exercise (5%), and V0 was greater in both the JS (9.0%) and BPT exercises (3.4%). The estimated 1RM value was higher in the MAX condition for both the squat (124.1 vs. 117.8 kg) and the bench press exercises (89.2 vs. 83.9 kg). High-velocity eccentric actions led to significantly higher MPV values, without compromising reliability values. The L-V profile and their derived parameters are substantially affected by eccentric velocity instructions. Standardized protocols using maximal eccentric velocities are suitable to assess athletes' maximal neuromuscular performances with reliable L-V profiles, which may complement the information obtained through the habitual CON protocol.

articles.title: A Supplement Dose Is Not a Nutrient Requirement: When the Same Units Answer Different Questions.
articles.authors: Takuya Omura
articles.abstract: Clinical nutrition guidelines often contain numbers that look directly comparable but answer different questions. A supplement dose, a therapeutic total-intake target, and a population reference intake can all be expressed in grams of the same nutrient, yet they do not represent the same quantity. The risk is not that one number is wrong; it is that the wrong inference is drawn from a number that is right. Using the Nutritional Management Guidelines for Sarcopenia and Frailty 2025 as a current illustration, this commentary distinguishes 3 inferential layers: an implementation regimen, a therapeutic nutrition target, and a dietary reference value. The guideline suggests approximately 20-25 g/day of high-quality protein supplementation with exercise when intake is insufficient, while acknowledging that a recommended total daily protein intake for older people with sarcopenia or frailty cannot yet be specified. These statements are compatible, not contradictory. Moving from a tested regimen to a therapeutic total-intake target requires additional evidence on baseline intake, amount consumed, achieved exposure, comparator exposure, co-interventions, modifiers, and safety. Moving further to a dietary reference value requires a broader evidentiary scope focused on usual intake, intake-response relationships, safety, and population applicability. Guidance should therefore state what each number represents and what additional evidence is required before that number is transferred to a different inferential layer.

articles.title: Heart rate variability and cortisol responses to acute low- and moderate-intensity exercise in stress-related exhaustion.
articles.authors: Jenny Kling, Örjan Ekblom, Robert Persson Asplund et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Exercise is commonly recommended to support stress regulation and mental health, yet it remains unclear whether these benefits translate to conditions characterized by prolonged stress and fatigue. The aims were to examine whether autonomic and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis responses to a single exercise bout differ between individuals with stress-related exhaustion and healthy controls, and whether responses vary by exercise intensity. METHODS: In a randomized, counterbalanced crossover design, 30 individuals with stress-related exhaustion (93.3% women; age 46.3 ± 5.89) and 29 healthy controls with a comparable age and sex distribution (93.1% women; age 45.5 ± 5.47) completed two 22-min cycling sessions at workloads corresponding to 40% (low intensity) and 55% (moderate intensity) of estimated maximal oxygen uptake (V̇O₂max) on separate occasions. Heart rate variability (HRV; RMSSD, SD2/SD1, LF/HF) and salivary cortisol were assessed pre-exercise, post-exercise, and 30 min post-exercise, with HRV also assessed during exercise. RESULTS: Compared with controls, individuals with stress-related exhaustion showed lower RMSSD overall, with the most apparent between-group differences observed during the post-exercise period. Within the exhaustion group, moderate- compared with low-intensity exercise was associated with lower RMSSD and higher SD2/SD1 and LF/HF, whereas no intensity effects were observed in controls. No between-group differences were observed in HRV during exercise. Cortisol analyses suggested overall group-related differences, without clear differences across time points. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest altered physiological stress-system regulation in stress-related exhaustion and highlight the post-exercise period and exercise intensity as important considerations when tailoring exercise recommendations for this population. The study was retrospectively registered on 05/30/2024 at Clinical Trials.gov, with trial registration number NCT06429423.

articles.title: Effects of cues to walk softly and quietly on gait mechanics during load carriage.
articles.authors: Caleb D Johnson, David J Zeppetelli, Cole A Dempsey et al.
articles.abstract: Walking with load carriage is a routine and necessary activity for many occupations and recreational athletes, however it induces significant physical strain, resulting in high rates of musculoskeletal injury. Gait alteration cues to run softly/quietly have been shown to reduce external forces related to injury in runners. However, the effects of these cues have yet to be explored for load carriage. 38 participants completed testing on an instrumented treadmill while kinematics were tracked via optical motion capture. Participants first completed a habitual load carriage trial (HAB) at a self-selected pace (1.23 ± 0.12 m/s) while carrying an 18 kg weighted vest. They were given a 5-min warm-up followed by data collection. Participants were then cued to modify their gait by walking "quietly and softly" (SOFT), using the same pace as for HAB. Outcome variables were averaged across 20 strides, including peak hip/knee/ankle joint internal sagittal and frontal plane moments, peaks/excursion in joint angles, double-stance time, stride length, and cadence. The SOFT condition resulted in decreased second peak hip abduction and peak knee flexion moments, and second peak vertical forces, but increased peak knee extension moments and first peak vertical forces (p < 0.05, Cohen's d≥0.5). Further, the SOFT condition resulted in increased peak flexion angles (hip/knee) and reduced extension/plantarflexion angles (hip/knee/ankle). Given the conflicting changes in external forces, the results do not support SOFT as a modification to reduce overall musculoskeletal injury risk during load carriage.

articles.title: Passive Hyperthermia Increases Neural Recruitment, Thereby Reducing Processing Efficiency During Executive Task Performance.
articles.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
articles.authors: Manabu Shibasaki, Shigehiko Ogoh, Kanoko Ito et al.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Heat-induced hyperthermia impairs cognitive performance and contributes to central fatigue during exercise and environmental heat exposure. Electroencephalographic event-related potential (EEG-ERP) studies consistently show reduced P300 amplitudes under heat stress, whereas functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies often report expanded blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) activation. PURPOSE: This study examined how passive hyperthermia influences task-dependent neural activation and cognitive processing using both fMRI and EEG-ERP within comparable paradigms. METHODS: Eighteen healthy adults (ten males and eight females) performed Go/No-go and Flanker tasks under normothermic and hyperthermic conditions during fMRI. Passive heating increased external ear canal temperature (Tear) by approximately 1.1°C above baseline. Sixteen participants completed an additional EEG-ERP session with the Flanker task. Behavioral responses, regional BOLD activation, and P300 amplitude and latency were assessed. Cervical arterial blood flow was measured by using a color-coded ultrasound system. RESULTS: The mean heating duration was 53.9 ± 9.2 min across all subjects. Hyperthermia increased heart rate and Tear while reducing internal carotid and vertebral artery blood flow. Reaction times decreased in both tasks, with no change in error rates. fMRI showed expanded activation in bilateral frontal, parietal, temporal, and subcortical regions. Task subtraction analyses (Flanker minus Go/No-go) revealed greater frontal and parietal activation during the complex task. In contrast, P300 amplitude was reduced during hyperthermia. CONCLUSION: Passive hyperthermia expands the spatial extent task-related BOLD activation while reducing P300 amplitude, suggesting reduced processing efficiency. However, the BOLD findings should be interpreted with caution because cerebral perfusion was also reduced. These findings suggest increased neural strain under heat stress, contributing to central fatigue and potentially impairing decision-making in sport and occupational setting.

articles.title: Portable Dynamometry Is Reliable for Measuring Knee and Ankle Strength in Daily Practice: Results From a Systematic Review With Meta-analysis and Evidence Gap Map Using the COSMIN Methodology.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: Rubén Gajardo-Burgos, Teresa Jaque de la Barra, Rodrigo Ramírez-Campillo et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To estimate the reliability and criterion validity of knee and ankle muscle strength measured using portable dynamometers. DESIGN: Systematic review with meta-analysis and evidence gap map. LITERATURE SEARCH: Systematic search of MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, SPORTDiscus, and Web of Science from inception to April 2025. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: We included studies that evaluated reliability or criterion validity of portable dynamometers for measuring knee extensor/flexor or ankle dorsiflexor/plantarflexor/invertor/evertor isometric strength in uninjured people or people with a lower-limb musculoskeletal condition. DATA SYNTHESIS: We performed meta-analyses for each muscle group, position, and fixation method. Methodological quality was assessed using the COSMIN (COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments) Risk of Bias tool. Certainty of evidence was graded using a modified GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluations) approach. RESULTS: We included 123 studies (n = 5042 participants); 113 studies were included in the meta-analysis. There was moderate- to high-certainty evidence of sufficient reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient ≥ 0.70) across most muscle groups, positions, and fixation methods. High-certainty evidence supported external fixation for assessing knee extensors/flexors and ankle plantarflexors. Evidence for criterion validity was sparse, and the certainty of evidence ranged from very low to high. There was high-certainty evidence of sufficient validity for knee extensor and flexor strength with external fixation in seated positions (r = 0.82-0.90). CONCLUSION: Portable dynamometers were sufficiently reliable for measuring isometric knee and ankle strength in clinical practice. The evidence for criterion validity was limited. Portable dynamometers should not yet be considered direct substitutes for isokinetic dynamometry. Reliability and validity estimates were consistent across uninjured and clinical populations. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):657-671. Epub 7 Jul 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14091.

articles.title: Tissue-Specific Regulation of Glucose and Lipid Metabolism by miR-29a in Insulin Resistance and Type 2 Diabetes.
articles.journal: American journal of physiology. Endocrinology and metabolism
articles.authors: Mariazel Rubio-Valles, Brendan Egan, Everardo Gonzalez-Rodriguez et al.
articles.abstract: MicroRNA-29a (miR-29a) has emerged as a context-dependent regulator of glucose and lipid metabolism in insulin-sensitive tissues, yet its tissue-specific actions in insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes remain incompletely understood. We synthesized peer-reviewed evidence retrieved from PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCOhost on the role of miR-29a across skeletal muscle, adipose tissue, liver, and pancreatic β-cells. We first define the nomenclature and genomic organization of the miR-29 family, its upstream transcriptional regulators, and the Argonaute-based evidence that separates direct target repression from correlative association. Across these tissues, miR-29a modulates oxidative metabolism, inflammatory signaling, and mitochondrial adaptation, largely through the PPARδ/PGC-1α axis, exerting complex and sometimes opposing effects depending on the tissue environment. We further examine miR-29a as a mediator of interorgan communication through extracellular vesicles, its responsiveness to exercise, and its emerging value as a biomarker and therapeutic target, while highlighting unresolved contradictions and translational hurdles. Because miR-29 family members act as tumor suppressors in most epithelial tissues, we also address the oncogenic risk inherent in nucleic acid strategies that lower miR-29a levels. Collectively, this mini-review positions miR-29a as a physiology-oriented integrator of metabolic remodeling and tissue-specific adaptation in metabolic disease.

articles.title: Visual external focus of attention modulates corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance after acute exercise.
articles.authors: Philipp Bauer, João H Oliveira, João S Gomes et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: Individuals are frequently instructed to adopt an internal focus during exercise, such as concentrating on a specific muscle, which may inadvertently lead to online conscious motor processing and constrain automatic motor control. In contrast, an external focus, particularly with distant visual feedback, is thought to benefit corticospinal modulation, enhancing automaticity and movement complexity. Nonetheless, the effective integration of attentional focus into evidence-based exercise prescription requires a mechanistic understanding of its neurophysiological basis. Therefore, this study investigated whether a single exercise bout performed with visual external, external or internal focus differentially modulates corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance (Corticospinal Excitability/Silent Period ratio), short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), intracortical facilitation (ICF) and torque complexity. METHODS: Thirty-seven healthy young adults were randomised to internal (12), external (12), or visual external focus (13) groups, completing a seated calf-raise bout to failure under the respective focus of attention instruction. Neurophysiological outcomes were assessed using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and analysed in a linear mixed-effects model. RESULTS: Corticospinal excitation-inhibition balance was enhanced after an exercise bout carried out with a visual external focus (increase 1.40 ± 0.42 mV/s, p = 0.005), while no changes were detected with an external or internal focus (all p ≥ 0.05). SICI, ICF and torque complexity showed no significant effect regarding attentional focus. CONCLUSION: The present study contributes to the neurophysiological basis for using goal-oriented visual feedback cues to increase corticospinal drive, offering a targeted intervention strategy which has potential to optimize motor performance in elite athletes and accelerate functional recovery in clinical populations. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: The present study was registered under NCT06538766 on 26/07/2024.

articles.title: The Effect of Environmental Temperature on Physical Performance, Physiological and Perceptual Responses in Elite Versus Nonelite Male Beach Soccer Players.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Thiago Carvalho, Vincenzo Rago, João Brito et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: High environmental temperature (Te) is associated with adverse effects on athletes' performance. Whether such effects are comparable across different sports and competitive levels remains uncertain. We explored and compared the physical performance, physiological, and perceptual responses of elite and nonelite beach soccer players during official matches, focusing on the potential effects of Te. METHODS: One hundred fifty-four male beach soccer players were monitored across 13 official matches. Physical performance (locomotor activity and countermovement jump), heart rate, rate of perceived exertion, hydration (liquid intake and fluid loss), and Te were collected. Data were analyzed using multivariate analysis of variance, followed by multivariate analysis of covariance and interaction analyses. RESULTS: Elite players covered greater total distance (∼16%), high-speed running (∼19%), and sprinting (∼60%); performed more sprints (∼60%) and had ∼1-point higher rate of perceived exertion than nonelite players. After adjustment for Te, differences in total distance and rate of perceived exertion between competitive levels appeared attenuated. In contrast, small effects were observed for Vpeak (ηp2=.037) and accelerations (ηp2=.030), and a medium effect was observed for fluid loss (ηp2=.076). As Te increased, elite players tended to cover greater total distance while reducing high-intensity actions, whereas nonelite players showed progressively greater high-intensity efforts, with relatively stable HRpeak and HRmean, while time >85%HRpeak tended to increase. In matches played at Te ≥ 35 °C, elite players experienced ∼34% greater fluid loss than nonelite players. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that elite and nonelite beach soccer players may respond differently as Te increases, highlighting the need for monitoring and hydration strategies tailored to competitive level under high Te conditions.

articles.title: Dietary Polysaccharides for Overweight and Obesity Management: Targeting AMPK via the Gut Microbiota and Metabolites-A Review.
articles.authors: Zhongxing Chu, Zuomin Hu, Baitong Zhu et al.
articles.abstract: Obesity arises from dietary energy intake-expenditure imbalance. 5'-Adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a core regulator of biological energy metabolism, is a key target for obesity research and can be activated by endogenous stimuli, such as cellular stress and physical exercise. As natural active components with diverse sources and biological functions, dietary polysaccharides have shown potential lipid-lowering and antiobesity effects in preclinical studies. This narrative review systematically summarizes their structural characteristics, sources, absorption-utilization mechanisms and structure-activity relationships, focusing on their regulatory effects on obesity via the AMPK pathway. We searched PubMed and Web of Science for publications (2014-2026) using "dietary polysaccharides,""AMPK,""obesity," and "gut microbiota" as key words, screening original studies and reviews relevant to the core topic. Correlative evidence suggests that dietary polysaccharides are associated with altered expression of lipid metabolism-related factors through potential modulation of gut microbiota and its metabolites, with indirect links to AMPK activation. Such AMPK regulatory effects have tissue/organ specificity, and the causal relationship of each link remains to be rigorously established. Notably, the majority of current evidence derives from in vitro and rodent models, and extrapolation to human obesity management requires caution, as high-quality human clinical trials are urgently needed to validate the translational potential of these preclinical findings. This review clarifies the potential mechanism and existing research gaps of dietary polysaccharides in obesity alleviation, providing a scientific basis for the research and development of lipid-lowering functional foods based on dietary polysaccharides.

articles.title: The Relationship of Countermovement Jump Performance to Operational Readiness in United States Air Force Special Operators.
articles.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
articles.authors: Sam T Tomlitz, Jay Dawes, Mark G Abel et al.
articles.abstract: Tomlitz, ST, Dawes, J, Abel, MG, and Potenza, MA. The relationship of countermovement jump performance to operational readiness in United States air force special operators. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Operational readiness signifies the degree to which special operations soldiers are physically capable of accomplishing occupational tasks. The purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between selected countermovement jump (CMJ)-derived neuromuscular performance characteristics and operational readiness assessment scores among United States Air Force Pararescuemen (PJs). Thirty-six male PJs (age = 37.06 ± 5.98 years, height = 178.73 ± 6.27 cm, body mass (BM) = 86.51 ± 8.97 kg, body mass index = 27.06 ± 2.24 kg/m2) performed a series of tests, including a CMJ test and components of the tier II Operator Fitness Test (OFT). The CMJ-derived metrics (jump height, concentric impulse (CI), reactive strength modified, peak power (PP), PP/BM, concentric peak force, peak landing force, landing impulse, CI asymmetry, countermovement depth, eccentric PP/BM, force at zero velocity) were correlated with the tier II OFT events using bivariate Spearman's correlations. The significance level of this study was set at ≤ 0.05. A large relationship was found between standing long jump and reactive strength index modified (RSImod) (rs = 0.62, p = 0.012). Multiple power variables correlated with farmer's carry sprint performance, including CI (rs = -0.59, p = 0.038), RSImod (rs = -0.64, p = 0.007), PP (rs = -0.71, p < 0.001), and relative PP (PP/BM) (rs = -0.74, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that specific performance characteristics may serve as useful indicators of task performance in the OFT assessment.

articles.title: What characteristics are associated with meeting the Canadian physical activity guidelines for people with multiple sclerosis? A retrospective chart review.
articles.journal: Applied physiology, nutrition, and metabolism = Physiologie appliquee, nutrition et metabolisme
articles.authors: Jillian Scandiffio, Sarah Munce, Sarah J Donkers et al.
articles.abstract: Meeting multiple sclerosis-specific physical activity guidelines (PAGs) has been associated with numerous benefits in people with multiple sclerosis (PwMS). However, the characteristics of PwMS predictive of meeting PAGs are unknown. This study aimed to examine which sociodemographic and clinical characteristics are associated with meeting the Canadian MS PAGs. A retrospective chart review of all PwMS referred to physiatry at the largest Canadian tertiary MS clinic between December 2021-December 2023 (n=455) was conducted. Physical activity, sociodemographic, and clinical characteristics were collected. Physical activity levels were categorized into one of three groups: no activity, some activity but not meeting PAGs, and meeting PAGs. Physical activity was further categorized by type of activity (aerobic and strength training). Associations between characteristics and physical activity levels were examined using multinomial logistic regression. PwMS who did not drive (OR=0.53, 95%CI=0.29-0.97) and were non-ambulatory (OR=0.34, 95%CI 0.11-0.99) were significantly less likely to meet PAGs. Higher Expanded Disability Status Scale (OR=0.80, 95% CI=0.70-0.91), gait aid use (OR=0.55, 95%CI=0.34-0.88), incoordination (OR= 0.52, 95% CI=0.33-0.82), progressive MS phenotype (OR=0.60, 95% CI=0.37-0.95), and smoking (OR=0.31, 95% CI=0.13-0.76) were associated with lower odds of doing any aerobic activity. Those with cognitive symptoms (OR=1.93, 95%CI=1.22-3.04) and greater muscle strength (OR=1.04, 95% CI=1.01-1.07) were more likely to do aerobic activity. Only employment status was associated with strength training, with those employed more likely to do some strength training (OR=1.73, 95% CI=1.04-2.89). Physical disability, cognitive symptoms, adverse health behaviours may drive which type and amount of activity a PwMS participates in.

articles.title: Effectiveness of Neuromuscular Training and Training Load Management Interventions for Reducing Injury and Attrition in Tactical Recruits: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis.
articles.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
articles.authors: James R Mckee, Bruna M Tessarin, Vanessa Sutton et al.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To estimate the effectiveness of neuromuscular training and training load management interventions for reducing injury and attrition in tactical personnel (military, law enforcement, and other first responder organizations) during recruit training. DESIGN: Intervention systematic review with meta-analysis. LITERATURE SEARCH: PubMed, CINAHL Plus with full text, EMBASE, CENTRAL, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus were searched from January 1, 2000, to March 14, 2025. STUDY SELECTION CRITERIA: Studies were included if they were quasi-experimental and randomized controlled trials examining neuromuscular training interventions conducted during or before commencing recruit training, or with training load management interventions, on medical-attention and time-loss injuries and attrition in tactical recruits aged at least 16 years. DATA SYNTHESIS: Inverse-variance, random-effects meta-analyses provided log odds ratio (Log OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). RESULTS: Thirty-three studies (n = 49,062 participants) were included, and outcomes were of very low-certainty. Neuromuscular training interventions delivered during recruit training reduced medical-attention injuries (Log OR = 0.520, 95% CI = 0.226 to 0.815), but not attrition (Log OR = 0.525, 95% CI = -0.292 to 1.342). Neuromuscular training interventions delivered before commencing recruit training did not reduce medical-attention injuries (Log OR = 0.487, 95% CI = -2.216 to 3.190) but could have significantly increased attrition (Log OR = -0.982, 95% CI = -1.874 to -0.090). Training load management interventions did not reduce medical-attention injuries (Log OR = 0.286, 95% CI = -0.183 to 0.755). CONCLUSION: Neuromuscular training interventions during recruit training may reduce medical-attention injury probability without increasing attrition. The lack of specificity and progressive overload for included interventions may have limited further protective effects against injury. Delivering neuromuscular training interventions before commencing recruit training may increase attrition during recruit training without affecting injury probability. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2026;56(10):642-656. Epub 18 August 2026. doi:10.2519/jospt.2026.14272.

articles.title: Initial Acceleration Deficit as a Timing-Derived Performance Metric of Early-Phase Sprint Acceleration in Elite Youth Soccer Players.
articles.journal: International journal of sports physiology and performance
articles.authors: Nikolaos Androulakis, Evaggelos Sideropoulos, Nikolaos Koundourakis
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To examine the applied relevance of initial acceleration deficit (IAD) as a timing-derived performance metric of early-phase sprint acceleration in elite youth soccer players. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted in 112 elite male youth soccer players (aged 15-18 y). Sprint performance was assessed over 25 m using dual-beam timing gates (splits at 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25 m). IAD was calculated as the difference between the 0- to 10- and 5- to 15-m intervals derived from the same trial. Vertical jump performance and anthropometric characteristics were also assessed. IAD was additionally expressed in normalized form, and percentile-based reference values (25th, 50th, and 75th) were established.
